What I found: measuring "dollar volume just hit a recent high" as the 5-day average of USDT volume divided by that coin's own 60-day average, the ratio is unit-free and comparable across coins, and it points the opposite way from the idea — coins whose volume recently peaked relative to their own history went on to underperform, with incremental IC of −0.0096 (t = −3.3) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 (−0.0151, −0.0150, −0.0014). The plain level-relative-to-its-own-history version was also negative, and the two readings are not different in content, so the effect is not a re-expression of liquidity or volatility. The direction is therefore against the idea rather than against the data, and I keep the direction the idea states.

The idea is about the size of the daily high-low range, which is a ratio of two prices and therefore comparable across coins. I'll measure it as the high minus the low divided by the close, smooth it over 5 days, and put a minus sign on the outside because the idea says wide range is bearish.

That reads well: incremental IC +0.0205 with t = 8.8 and the same positive sign in all three periods. One thing worth checking is whether the ratio form is the right one — the range as a share of the close is a ratio, so it is bounded; the range as a share of the day's range (high-low divided by high-low) is a pure scale, which is a cleaner measure of "how wide this day's range is".

The ratio form (range over day's range) is not the right one: it is nearly zero on most days and gives no incremental information, so the plain range-to-close ratio is the one I keep.

The idea says dollar-denominated turnover is bearish, so I'll start with the simplest form: average daily USDT turnover over the last 20 days, which is comparable across coins because it's a ratio of USDT to coin value.

The plain 20-day average came out at −0.0011 with the sign flipping between periods, so the raw level of turnover doesn't carry the signal. The idea is about "trading very little" rather than about the level of turnover, so I'll try a rank-based version: each coin's 20-day average dollar volume ranked within its own 60-day history, so the factor is a stable coin-specific measure of how unusually light-traded the coin is.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. The level of dollar turnover is a negative predictor of next-day returns (rank IC −0.0371, t = −1.9, and it is negative in all three sub-periods), and after removing the known liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum styles the incremental part is essentially zero (−0.0011, t = −1.9). The rank-based version, which is supposed to measure "unusually light" rather than the level, came out clearly worse (−0.0046) and flips sign across periods, so it is not the same signal. The effect is real but very small and it points the other way from the idea: coins with higher dollar turnover did slightly better over the following days. I am keeping the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign to chase the data.

A 1-day return is the same coin-by-coin as the 1-day return already removed, so this is a different measure from the 1-day return; I'll start with the simplest version of it.

The range-scaled version is indistinguishable from the raw up-move (−0.0000, t = −0.0), so it is not a different reading of the same thing. The idea simply does not hold on this history: close-to-open up-moves are followed by weaker returns, and that is not an artifact of the known styles being subtracted.

The most direct form is the close's position inside the range, i.e. `(close - high)/(close - low)`, which is a pure price-ratio so it is comparable across coins regardless of price level. I'll start with the simplest version, a 10-day mean of that position, since a single day's position is noisy.
